newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine army told to play down fighting in south.
newsitem.headline: Philippine army told to play down fighting in south.

text.p: The armed forces have ordered field commanders to play down reports of fighting with Moslem rebels, saying they gave the Philippines a bad name before this month's APEC summit, military sources said on Monday.

They said the order came from military headquarters in Manila last week shortly before guerrillas ambushed an army patrol in Tipo-Tipo town on the southern island of Basilan, killing seven soldiers and wounding 10.

The military high command is concerned that the uncontrolled release of information on the fighting may give a negative impression of the Philippines to delegates to the November 25 summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, said the sources, who asked not to be identified.
"We'll get clubbed in the media if this memo gets out," one officer who was aware of the directive, told reporters.
Two other senior military officers, also asking not to be identified, confirmed there was such a memorandum.

"We just want to maintain the system of releasing information through the PIO (the military's public information office). We don't want our field commanders to be taken out of context and they don't have a complete picture of the situation," one general said.
"We have visitors coming and erroneous, irresponsible media reports create a bad picture about our country," another general said.
"It's best to be discreet about these things and to relay only those that are essential and necessary," the officer added.
The killings brought to 13 the number of soldiers who have died since fighting began in mid-October against elements of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).

Military estimates of MILF dead ranged up to 50, but officers said this was based on intercepted rebel radio messages, bloodstains found in the tracks of retreating guerrillas and reports from villagers about rebels carrying their casualties with them in their retreat.
Residents told reporters who visited Tipo-Tipo over the weekend that the military had declared 10 villages in the municipality "off limits" to civilians.
This was apparently to prevent civilians from getting caught in the crossfire, they said.
More than 4,000 villagers comprising about 700 families have fled their homes in the 10 villages since the fighting started.
About 2,000 soldiers, including crack Marine units, are involved in the operation against an estimated 350 MILF men.
The MILF is a hardline guerrilla faction demanding an Islamic state and is not part of a peace deal signed last month between Manila and the mainstream Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF).
The peace accord ended a 24-year, MNLF-led revolt for Moslem autonomy in the southern islands.
The fighting in Tipo-Tipo erupted while the government was conducting exploratory talks with MILF officers to try to negotiate a separate deal with them.
